title: Comet and Juniper's Magnetic Mystery
markdown:
Sunbeams dappled through the leaves and painted the forest floor. Comet the mole, fur the colour of rich soil, blinked his tiny eyes. He loved to dig, but his biggest joy was finding things that sparkled or felt smooth and mysterious. Today he and his friend Juniper the robin had stumbled on a grand pile: sparkly mica that winked like tiny stars, cool colourful river stones, and lots of dull grey pebbles.

“Oh, Comet,” chirped Juniper, voice like a tiny cheerful bell, red breast puffed. “Look at all these treasures. But how will we know which ones are truly special? Some sparkle, and then these other stones sparkle too.” She nudged a dull pebble with her beak. It did not sparkle at all.

Comet pushed a shiny piece of mica with his paw. It shimmered, but so did other bits that were only colourful stone. “It is so hard to tell,” he mumbled, nose twitching. “Some are shiny. Some are just ordinary grey.” He sighed, a little puff of dust. Sorting the pile felt like counting stars on a cloudy night. His whiskers drooped.

Then Juniper spotted something nestled under a mossy root. “What’s this, Comet?”

The stone was unlike the others: smooth and dark as the deepest night, cool and solid. Comet shuffled over, whiskers interested, mole nose sniffing. As Juniper leaned in, a tiny iron nail, fallen from an old bird’s nest high above, slipped from her beak. It tumbled and landed with a soft tap not far from the dark stone.

Zing. The little iron nail sprang from the ground, as if pulled by an invisible string, and clanked onto the side of the dark stone.

Juniper’s wings fluttered. “Did you see that? It just flew.”

Comet nudged the nail. It wiggled, then stuck fast, as if glued. He picked up another tiny iron nail from the pile and held it near. Zip. It leaped and clung. Comet’s eyes widened. Juniper hopped in amazement.

“It’s pulling them,” Comet whispered. “The stone is pulling the nails.”

Juniper hopped around it, delighted. “Maybe we can use this special stone to help us sort.”

Comet nodded. They mixed the tiny iron nails back among the dull pebbles and glittering stones. Then, with great care, Comet brought the dark stone close.

Clink, clank, zip, zing. One by one the iron nails leaped from the pile and stuck fast to the dark stone. Soon all the nails were gathered there, leaving the dull pebbles and the other glittering treasures neatly apart.

Comet pawed the nails, muffled with delight. Juniper fluttered from pile to pile.

“It is like—” Juniper began, then stopped, head tilted.

Comet looked at the nails sticking firmly. He tilted his head. His little mole brain worked. “It is not a trick,” he said. “It is a special kind of pull. This stone does not pull everything. It only pulls certain things, like these iron nails. A force you cannot see, but you can feel.” He tapped one of the nails. “This pull has a name. Magnetism. This dark stone is a magnet.”

That was when it clicked for Juniper too. The mica still winked. The river stones stayed cool and unmoved. Only the iron had come.

As the sun began to dip, long soft shadows stretched. Comet and Juniper looked at their sorted treasures with new understanding.

“I wonder,” Juniper chirped, eyes twinkling, “what other hidden pulls and pushes are all around us, waiting to be discovered. Are there other special stones? Other invisible forces?”

Comet nosed the magnet once more, gentle, as if it might still have something to say. The forest held its quiet, full of things that did not sparkle and still mattered, and the two of them were already listening for the next unseen tug.
